st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s case for task-specific, human-supervised augmentation. Its experiment shows that efficiency depends on interface design—highlighting alone outperformed highlighting plus summaries—and it frames likely adoption as guidance for human decision-makers rather than autonomous determination. It does not address the cluster’s broader claims about direct-to-consumer verification risks, remedies or inequality.
qs: AI summaries and AI highlighting together improved efficiency but not as much as AI highlighting alone.

We study how the process and outputs of legal work may be impacted by new AI tools, a topic of particular importance since most new legal AI adoption is likely to reflect a “human in the loop” model, wherein AI does not directly determine outcomes but instead provides guidance to human decision makers (Mosqueira-Rey et al., 2022).

st.t: Legal productivity: Speed gains exceed quality gains
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s central finding that legal AI can produce substantial speed gains without measurable quality improvement, while materially extending it by experimentally isolating assistance formats. It shows that highlighting accelerated complaint review by about 30%, whereas summaries reduced or eliminated that advantage, strengthening the case for task- and output-specific evaluation rather than blanket productivity claims.
qs: Discussion We find that the right kind of AI assistance can speed up the average rate of task completion on a realistic legal task while not affecting the means or distributions of measurements of the quality of legal work and process.
Rather we here experimentally demonstrate the importance of calibrating the amount and form of AI assistance provided during human-machine cooperation to complete a legal task.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s supervised, task-specific augmentation framing and materially strengthens it with randomized evidence that one bounded form of assistance reduced completion time without lowering measured quality, while another offered no benefit. Its explicit task limitation and human-in-the-loop orientation reinforce the cluster’s emphasis on selective workflow design rather than general legal autonomy or lawyer replacement.
qs: Compared to no AI assistance, AI-generated highlighting reduced task completion time by 30% without any reduction in measured quality indicators.

We do not argue that highlighting is a better intervention for all legal outcomes; we show only that highlighting enhances efficiency without introducing distortions into legal work for the specific task studied here.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source accepts human-in-the-loop augmentation and materially strengthens the cluster’s claim that productivity gains are task- and workflow-dependent. Its randomized experiment adds observed causal evidence that AI can improve efficiency while showing that more assistance is not necessarily better: highlighting alone outperformed highlighting combined with summaries. It does not address verification costs or junior staffing directly.
qs: Our results show that AI support can dramatically increase the efficiency of legal task completion, but finding the optimal form of AI assistance is a fine-tuning exercise.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s task- and context-specific account of productivity by reporting a statistically significant 29.7% completion-time reduction from highlighting-only assistance in a student legal task. kp.k: Randomized experiment tests assistance on junior-like legal tasks
kp.d: The authors studied 206 law students from nine U.S. law schools, collecting data from January to April 2022. A randomized between-subjects 2 × 2 design assigned no AI, summaries only, highlighting only, or both. Participants reviewed the same three complaints in the same order, answered factual and legal retrieval questions, and assessed merits. The authors frame these tasks as analogous to junior associates' and law clerks' initial complaint review, rather than autonomous AI lawyering.
qs: Data was collected via snowball sampling from January to April
Within that flow, participants were assigned on a between-subjects randomized basis to any of four treatments

Reading a complaint document and recalling or retrieving information from that complaint is analogous to many real-world legal work experiences, particularly those of junior law clerks or junior law firm associates

kp.d: Highlighting Only participants took a mean 941 seconds, versus 1,338 seconds without AI, a 29.7% reduction across the three document tasks. The post hoc comparison was significant (Wilcoxon p < .01; t-test p = .01). Timing excluded consent, the exit survey, and transitions. This is observed task-level efficiency evidence, not a measured change in firm-wide productivity, staffing, or prices.
qs: The mean times to complete the experiment ranged from under 16 minutes (941 s) for the Highlighting Only group to over 22 minutes (1,338 s) for the No AI treatment, reflecting a 29.7% reduction in task completion time for the Highlighting Only group.
This difference between Highlighting Only and No AI was significant, (post hoc, Wilcoxon, p < .01; ttest, p = .01)

kp.k: More AI assistance was not necessarily better
kp.d: Summaries alone did not improve performance relative to no AI; completion times were statistically equivalent using a Cohen's d = .5 equivalence bound. Combining summaries and highlighting improved efficiency less than highlighting alone. The Highlighting Only versus Full AI timing comparison reached only p < .1 on both reported tests. The authors therefore recommend task-specific calibration of output form and quantity rather than assuming additional assistance increases benefits.
qs: AI-generated summaries produced no change in performance metrics compared to no AI assistance.
AI summaries and AI highlighting together improved efficiency but not as much as AI highlighting alone.
A two-one sided t-test confirms that Summary Only and No AI are statistically equivalent (p < .05, Cohen’s d = .5).
Rather we here experimentally demonstrate the importance of calibrating the amount and form of AI assistance provided during human-machine cooperation to complete a legal task.

kp.k: Speed gains showed no measured accuracy penalty
kp.d: Mean textual-question accuracy ranged from 85.4% (SD 14.6%) with Full AI to 87.7% (SD 12.5%) with Summary Only. The highest and lowest groups were statistically equivalent at a medium effect-size bound (post hoc p < .01, Cohen's d = .5). Pairwise accuracy distributions and rates of at least 95% accuracy also showed no significant treatment differences. The authors nevertheless acknowledge that the sample could miss smaller quality effects.
qs: The mean accuracy in responding to the textual questions was strikingly similar
ranging from M = 85.4% (SD = 14.6%) in the Full AI condition to M = 87.7% (SD = 12.5%) in the Summary Only condition.
It could be, however, that the null effect of the AI manipulation in this experiment is a result of the small sample size rather than a true null.

kp.k: Judgment and diligence proxies showed no treatment effects
kp.d: Complaint merits ratings varied by document, not AI treatment. Freeform-response character counts, Flesch-Kincaid grade levels, and ROUGE-1 overlap with complaints likewise showed no systematic treatment effects. Scrolling to the document's empirically defined end was also unaffected. The authors interpret these as evidence against reduced effort or distorted judgment, while explicitly treating several measures as proxies rather than comprehensive assessments of legal work quality.
qs: We find no difference in exercise of judgment or responsibility across treatments.
Across all three effort proxies, we see that the experimental AI treatments did not systematically bias participants’ chosen effort level.

Participants’ exercise of some minimal level of professional responsibility – in this case by looking at the whole legal complaint before offering a quality assessment – was unaffected by the presence of either form of AI assistance.

kp.k: Attention-based highlighting repurposed an existing commercial model
kp.d: The tool was already used commercially to help legal editors produce complaint summaries. Highlight darkness represented word-level attention values generated during summary production, not a model trained specifically to help participants answer the experiment's questions. The authors regard the successful transfer from specialist editorial work to less specialized complaint review as evidence that useful assistance can come from repurposing existing AI outputs.
qs: The darker the highlighting, the larger the numerical attention value generated for that word, which in turn indicated that the word had been more influential in shaping the model’s outputs in constructing the one-sentence summary of the complaint.

The highlighting being helpful was especially unexpected considering it was not trained with the intention of being helpful to humans, but rather is a byproduct of training the AI to produce one sentence summaries.

We took an AI product trained for one task and one population (to assist expert attorney employees in producing publishable one sentence summaries of complaint documents) and tested it on another task and another population.

kp.k: Selected high-quality outputs limit conclusions about unreliable AI
kp.d: The experiment deliberately selected complaints whose summaries both attorney raters considered publication-ready: 58 of 100 supplied documents qualified, while 91 were approved by at least one rater. Final documents and questions were selected without knowledge of the summaries or highlighting, and overly long documents were excluded to avoid exceeding model capacity. Consequently, the study tests assistance of a presumptively good standard, not how users handle erroneous outputs or general model reliability.
qs: We limited our selection of complaints to those for which the model produced an output that was judged publication-ready by both of two attorney raters.
58 out of 100 documents were rated by both attorneys as publication-ready, while 91 out of 100 were rated as such by at least one attorney reviewer.
We therefore cannot and do not put forward any assertions regarding the quality of the model outputs generally.

kp.d: Post hoc tests found neither better answers specifically where correct information was highlighted nor altered distributions of correct and incorrect responses. An added confidence question, answered by 68 participants, showed no significant treatment differences in self-assessed performance; self-assessment predicted accuracy. The authors find no evidence for confidence bias, but do not establish the mechanism. They speculate that sufficiently binding time limits could convert observed time savings into accuracy advantages.
qs: While our experiment does not definitively answer this question, we present some circumstantial evidence that tends to rule out possibilities relating to the information content of the highlighting.
we found no difference in the distribution of responses, correct or incorrect, to any individual question among the different experimental treatments
However, we found no evidence for this or other affective mechanisms that might work through biasing confidence.
In other words, we would expect, under time pressure, that participants with highlighting should demonstrate higher accuracy than participants without highlighting.

kp.k: Professional and long-term generalization requires further testing
kp.d: Participants were law students, not practicing attorneys; the authors report prior studies showing that student and judicial behavior can differ. There was no imposed time limit, compensation was a flat $20, and outcomes came from one session. Workplace time pressure and repeated use could change effects. The authors explicitly characterize the findings as task-specific proof of possibility, allowing that summaries might outperform highlighting for other tasks such as identifying relevant precedent.
qs: There was no time limit
Compensation for participating was $20 for all participants regardless of how quickly or correctly they completed the experiment.
In this experiment, we looked at short-term outcomes during a single experimental session.
Our conclusions should be interpreted as a demonstration of possibility rather than a guarantee of success of AI for enhancing legal work efficiency.
It is quite likely that for other legal tasks, another form of AI assistance would be superior.

kp.k: Earlier verification study supports output-specific experimentation
kp.d: The authors report Norkute et al. (2021), a separate study of the same tool in which two specialized legally trained employees checked summaries for correctness and writing quality. Attention-based highlighting reduced review time from 148 to 83 seconds per complaint, a 44% reduction, while abstractive highlighting did not. They emphasize the earlier study's two-person sample, specialized task, and absence of a numerical quality measure as reasons for the present larger experiment.
qs: The attention-based highlighting reduced the task completion time from 148 seconds to 83 seconds per complaint document, a 44% reduction, whereas abstractive highlighting failed to reduce task completion time.
The limited sample size (two attorneys) and the task at hand (producing one-sentence summaries of complaints for a proprietary legal subscription service) limit the external validity.

kp.k: Human deployment can defeat theoretical algorithmic benefits
kp.d: The literature review contrasts private-practice efficiency with criminal-justice risk assessment, where human discretion often produced mixed or null effects. The authors report that a 22-study meta-analysis covering more than 1.4 million people lost its significant reduction in restrictive placements after problematic studies were excluded. They also contrast Virginia findings of no overall incarceration reduction and demographic differences with Travis County findings of less punitive outcomes without exacerbated racial disparities. These are reported prior findings, not results of the complaint experiment.
qs: Once the problematic studies were removed from the meta-analysis, there was no statistically significant effect of AI assistance on reducing restrictive placements.
This study provides evidence that AI integrated into human decisions may produce results quite different from the outputs of the AI system alone.
In short, both observational and experimental studies of risk instruments suggest that the gains of algorithms have probably been minimal in practice in the criminal justice system.

kp.k: Authors recommend interface development and broader quality evaluation
kp.d: The authors recommend prioritizing highlighting capabilities, which they describe as not readily available from consumer-facing state-of-the-art LLMs at the time of writing. Their methodological contribution is a reusable behavioral-testing interface and a rubric combining accuracy, speed, discretionary judgment, effort, and reading-process measures. They propose that efficient human-in-the-loop assistance could improve access to legal services and justice, but do not measure access outcomes in this experiment.
qs: Currently, AI-generated highlighting is not readily available from state-of-the-art, consumer-facing large language models, but our work suggests that this capability should be prioritized in the development of legal AI products.
We develop and offer to the community a reusable interface into which AI outputs can be inserted for behavioral testing.
we put forward a simple rubric for evaluating AI assistance in legal tasks upon which future research can build.

our findings suggest reason for optimism and rapid adoption of forms of AI assistance known to enhance efficiency and therefore likely to prove helpful in increasing access to legal work and to the justice system.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Nielsen, Skylaki, Norkute and Stremitzer claim that carefully chosen AI assistance can substantially accelerate a specific legal task without reducing measured quality; more assistance is not necessarily better.
pts.d: The authors report that attention-based highlighting reduced complaint-review task completion time by 29.7% compared with no AI. Summaries alone did not change performance, while summaries combined with highlighting improved efficiency less than highlighting alone. They found no treatment effects on factual accuracy, assessments of complaint merits, proxies for effort in written explanations, or scrolling to the end of documents. They frame these findings as support for tailoring AI outputs to particular tasks rather than treating AI as a single intervention. They recommend prioritizing highlighting capabilities in legal AI products. Separately, they predict that highlighting could improve accuracy under sufficiently strong time pressure, and suggest that efficiency-enhancing assistance could expand access to legal work and justice. These latter claims are expectations, not demonstrated outcomes of the main experiment.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The primary evidence is a randomized experiment with 206 law students using outputs from a commercially deployed legal editorial AI tool.
pts.d: Participants were randomly assigned between subjects to no AI, summary only, highlighting only, or both forms of assistance. They reviewed the same three complaints in the same order. Mean completion times were 941 seconds with highlighting alone and 1,338 seconds without AI. The highlighting-versus-no-AI comparison was significant in post hoc tests (Wilcoxon p < .01; t-test p = .01); highlighting versus both forms of assistance was reported at p < .1. Mean textual accuracy ranged from 85.4% to 87.7% across groups. The authors used equivalence testing with a medium-effect-size bound and found no treatment effects on additional judgment and behavioral indicators. Those indicators included explanation length, reading-grade level, text overlap and scrolling behavior, rather than comprehensive expert assessment of legal work. The study was preregistered without directional hypotheses, and several reported analyses were post hoc. ETH funded implementation and participant compensation; Thomson Reuters supplied proprietary-tool access and two coauthors' participation. The authors also cite Norkute et al. (2021), in which two legally trained employees completed summary verification faster with attention-based highlighting, and a parallel study of the same participant pool that found no shift in proportional attention allocation. These are supporting studies, not additional independent evidence from practicing lawyers in the present experiment.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The demonstrated effects are short-term, task-specific findings from data collected in January–April 2022; the authors explicitly limit extrapolation to routine professional practice.
pts.d: The paper was published in 2024, but the experiment used an older, specialized commercial model rather than contemporary consumer-facing LLMs. Participants completed a single session without a time limit and received flat compensation. The authors selected complaints whose summaries both attorney raters considered publication-ready and excluded documents exceeding the model's input capacity. Thus, the study concerns presumptively good assistance, not exposure to unreliable outputs. The authors acknowledge that the sample may not detect smaller quality effects, law students may differ from professionals, real-world time pressure may change results, and repeated use might diminish or increase benefits. Their accuracy prediction under time pressure remains conditional; a footnote reports a pilot in which time pressure did not eliminate timing differences, not a demonstrated accuracy advantage. Their expectation of near-term adoption concerns human-in-the-loop assistance rather than replacement of human decision-makers. The statement about consumer-facing models lacking readily available highlighting is explicitly limited to the time of writing.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate subjects are law students performing work analogous to junior legal roles; proposed beneficiaries include legal professionals, legal AI developers and people seeking legal assistance.
pts.d: The authors position complaint reading, factual retrieval and preliminary assessment as representative of work done by junior law clerks and junior law-firm associates. The demonstrated benefit is faster completion while humans retain responsibility for answers and judgments, not autonomous legal service delivery or job displacement. The underlying tool already assists legal editors producing complaint summaries. Product developers are urged to test specific output formats and prioritize useful highlighting rather than assume that adding features improves performance. The authors suggest that efficiency gains may expand access to legal work and the justice system, but do not measure client prices, unmet civil legal need, service availability or distribution of savings. They offer no quantified prediction about law-firm employment, staffing leverage, billing models or legal-market shares.
